title: Invasive appendiceal adenocarcinoma after complete specimen review
fairness: Right hemicolectomy with regional nodes is the single best offered plan: the full specimen demonstrates infiltrative malignant glands extending into mesoappendiceal fat, staging does not demonstrate peritoneal or distant disease, and the patient is fit. A clear appendiceal base does not settle regional nodal management.

The two consequential steps are recognizing that a limited low-grade tip sample does not characterize the separate invasive proximal focus, then distinguishing regional oncologic resection from either surveillance or a peritoneal-treatment pathway. These are standard, testable appendiceal-neoplasm distinctions.

The words 'Expert permanent review of the entire specimen' establish sampling scope; they do not uniquely match an option. 'No distant lesions or deposits on serosal surfaces' is necessary staging information, not an unfair diagnosis giveaway. Options have comparable operative specificity and no convergence or absolute-wording shortcut was identified.

The follow-up coherently supplies the intervening appendectomy, complete pathology, staging and recovery. It stands alone with its presentation and update. The preceding exploration explanation does not teach the tumor operation.

This is an offline editorial judgment from the supplied candidate text, not fresh guideline verification or clinical approval. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified; Melissa's exact-version clinical review remains necessary. The same verification limitation applies throughout this report.
suggestions: Retain the complete-specimen versus tip-sample distinction, clear-margin finding and staging information; removing those would weaken the intended competing decisions.

title: Colonic evaluation after an appendiceal abscess
clarityIssues: 'An earlier luminal report' does not identify the procedure, documented extent, preparation quality or reason it ended. A reader cannot tell whether this was sigmoidoscopy, incomplete colonoscopy or an incomplete transferred record of a complete colonoscopy.

The last photographed landmark and locations of biopsy specimens do not by themselves establish the maximal extent examined. A complete colonoscopy can have distal biopsies, and missing proximal photographs do not prove that the cecum was never examined.

'Now before definitive resection planning' leaves the sequence of repeat CT versus colonoscopy partly implicit while the presentation still describes inflammatory thickening obscuring the lesion's origin.

cues.phrase: Its final photographed landmark is the descending colon, and biopsy labels identify rectum and sigmoid.
cues.why: This conspicuous omission points toward completing a colon examination, but the offered evidence is not sufficient to establish incompleteness. It risks rewarding an inference from absent documentation rather than interpretation of an actual procedure record.

fairness: Evaluating a possible underlying or synchronous colonic neoplasm after an older adult's appendiceal abscess is high yield. The intended two steps are determining what the prior examination actually assessed, then choosing the missing preoperative evaluation.

Colonoscopy is a plausible best plan, but the explanation overstates what the supplied record proves when it says the previous report covers 'not the cecum'. The record must distinguish an incomplete examination from incomplete documentation before that can be the decisive rationale.

Repeat CT after inflammatory resolution also addresses an explicitly unresolved and clinically relevant question. It need not replace colonoscopy, but the item should establish why colonoscopy is the next action at this particular visit rather than imply the two investigations are mutually exclusive.

No confident error in the general neoplasm-workup principle is alleged. The concern is the missing procedural evidence and exact sequencing, which should be resolved clinically rather than by inventing a waiting interval.

This revised version is standalone. It supplies its own post-abscess history and does not require the preserved interval-appendectomy companion. Its explanation must not be treated as automatically preserving that older companion's sequence acceptance.
suggestions: Identify the prior procedure and state its documented maximal insertion site and relevant adequacy findings. For example, use a procedure report that explicitly records termination in the descending colon, with a clinically credible reason; do not use distal biopsy labels as proof of examination extent.
Establish the clinical phase and the unresolved mucosal question sufficiently to rank colonoscopy now against delayed anatomic reassessment. Do not add an unsupported numerical waiting rule.

Rewrite the explanation to distinguish documented examination limits from missing records, and explicitly keep colonic mucosal assessment separate from later localization of a mural appendiceal lesion.

title: Initial resection extent for an appendiceal lesion involving adjacent cecum
clarityIssues: 'Partial cecectomy including the appendiceal base' does not explicitly say that the entire unresected appendix and its distended body are removed. In an item specifically testing resection extent, the reader should not have to infer that the intended operation is an en bloc appendectomy with a cecal cuff.

The explanation refers to 'affected cecal wall' without distinguishing observed gross thickening from proven neoplastic involvement. No tissue has been sampled. This wording can blur gross extent and tumor biology.
fairness: The intended limited en bloc resection is plausible given gross extension onto a small cecal patch separate from the valve, no demonstrated dissemination, and no histologic diagnosis establishing invasive cancer. I do not identify a confident clinical error in that intended plan; the exact operative label needs repair.

The useful reasoning is to map what an appendix-only division would leave behind, then distinguish a local diagnostic resection from an automatic regional nodal operation. The clear description of the cecal patch is decision-critical anatomy, not a word-overlap cue to remove.

All choices are at the initial resection stage. 'Every proposed resection would use intact handling and protected retrieval' appropriately makes handling common to the options instead of giving that safety advantage only to the key.

This is a high-yield distinction between local removal of a suspected appendiceal lesion and oncologic extension after characterization. Wall thickening alone should not be taught as proof either of neoplasia or of its histologic category.
The standalone presentation supplies age, sex, prior laparoscopy, unresected status and absence of a tissue diagnosis. There is no missing preceding result or feedback leak.
suggestions: Name the intended operation explicitly, such as 'En bloc appendectomy with a cecal cuff', with parallel labels for appendix-only removal and right hemicolectomy. Make clear that the complete appendix and the grossly abnormal adjacent patch are included.

Describe the resection as encompassing the gross abnormality for permanent histology. Avoid converting wall thickening into a proven histologic finding, and retain the statement that subsequent oncologic decisions depend on characterization.

title: Site-specific pathology and mucinous peritoneal disease
fairness: The diaphragmatic nodule contains mucinous epithelium at a separate peritoneal site. The negative pelvic nodule and clear appendiceal margin do not invalidate that positive specimen. This interpretation changes the relevant disease field and supports specialist assessment for cytoreduction and intraperitoneal therapy.

The key is an assessment pathway, not an assertion that immediate cytoreduction or HIPEC is mandatory despite no bulky residual disease. The explanation preserves that important distinction. Follow-up may ultimately be selected by the specialist team, but it should not be predetermined from the negative pelvic specimen and postoperative imaging.

The two steps are resolving the site-specific sampling evidence, then selecting peritoneal-disease assessment rather than regional colectomy or a preselected observation pathway. Appendiceal mucinous peritoneal spread is a standard board-relevant concept even though the clinical condition is uncommon.

All three options share 'Multidisciplinary review for' and name a concrete subsequent pathway. No uniquely cautious generic key, meaningful length outlier, absolute wording or nonmedical convergence shortcut was identified. The mucin and epithelial descriptions require medical interpretation rather than directly repeating an answer label.
The case is standalone and includes the operative specimens, complete primary review and postoperative staging. No earlier explanation is needed to establish the separate diaphragmatic finding.
suggestions: Retain 'assessment' rather than guaranteed treatment in the explanation. Preserve the separate specimen labels; combining them into a global negative or positive summary would remove the interpretation being tested.

title: Appendiceal NET resection after characterization of liver lesions

cues.why: Minor preinterpretation: 'resolves' announces that the prior uncertainty has been settled before the learner reads the morphology. It does not reveal whether the lesions are benign or metastatic and does not independently select the key, so this is an optional tightening rather than a blocking cue.

fairness: The MRI observations support simple cysts rather than a liver-biopsy requirement. The complete specimen then supplies a 2.6-cm well-differentiated NET, a clear base and a fit patient without demonstrated metastatic disease. Right hemicolectomy with regional nodes is the best offered plan under the usual size-based surgical teaching; no confident clinical inaccuracy was identified in this supplied scenario.

There are two consequential decisions: update the indeterminate CT findings using the acquired MRI morphology, then apply regional-resection reasoning despite favorable grade and a clear local margin. Incorrectly treating the lesions as unresolved changes the immediate action to biopsy; incorrectly equating a clear margin with adequate nodal treatment changes the action to follow-up.

The known neuroendocrine diagnosis is legitimate for a staging-and-management question. There is no need to hide it. The numerical tumor size is actual case data, not an invented probability or cutoff introduced by this review.

This is a standalone revision. Its presentation and update carry both the initial CT concern and the later MRI/pathology findings, with no dependence on the parked receptor-staging question. No preceding explanation supplies the MRI interpretation.
Appendiceal NET operative management is high yield. The liver imaging adds a meaningful staging issue rather than an unrelated second objective.
suggestions: For cleaner interpretation, replace 'resolves both previously indeterminate lesions' with a neutral statement that the MRI evaluates those same two lesions, followed by the current observations.
Remove 'directly sourced' from learner-facing feedback. Explain the clinical principle there and keep provenance language in the evidence records.

title: Reviewing an archived postoperative CT acquisition
clarityIssues: 'On this acquisition and transfer record' is awkward lead-in wording. The intended request is understandable, but the long update shifts most of the reading burden to file-transfer logistics.
Creatinine within its reference interval and absence of a prior contrast reaction do not determine whether already acquired images should be reviewed; those details add little to this exact decision.

cues.phrase: the source archive contains the complete postcontrast dataset, available for current radiologist review
cues.why: This effectively states the keyed action and its feasibility. A nonmedical reader can choose to review the explicitly available completed work rather than repeat it or obtain a different study.

cues.phrase: Review the archived contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT
cues.why: The key uniquely echoes both the archive and review language. The alternatives both acquire new images, so the option set reinforces the ordinary retrieve-before-redo shortcut.

cues.phrase: Symptoms and examination have not changed since that acquisition.
cues.why: This is legitimate information for fairness, but in combination with the complete available acquisition it removes the remaining practical reason to consider new imaging. The task then has little clinical discrimination. Do not simply delete it while keeping the same key.

fairness: Reviewing the available complete current contrast CT is the defensible best option. The record appropriately distinguishes an acquired dataset from the subset transferred, and no confident clinical inaccuracy is identified in this recommendation.

The exact tested skill is identifying a transferred-image subset and retrieving the missing completed work. The learner need not infer the postoperative diagnosis, select a clinically appropriate imaging protocol, or interpret an image. Calling record reconciliation and retrieval two clinical steps would overstate the difficulty.

Postoperative abscess localization is high yield, but this exact archive-versus-repeat decision is not itself a commonly tested appendicitis/ABSITE concept. Its clinical importance does not establish the requested resident-level testability.

The initial node stands alone. Its explanation does not disclose catheter drainage or the antibiotic endpoint, so later nodes can still assess distinct decisions. An easy first node does not invalidate those later tasks, but neither does the sequence make this node difficult.
suggestions: Move the archive retrieval into unscored setup and score a consequential interpretation or management decision using the actual returned information. Avoid duplicating the existing drainage objective merely to retain another scored node.
Alternatively, seek explicit acceptance of a basic record-scope teaching role; label its ease honestly instead of presenting it as a difficult clinical item.

Do not manufacture difficulty by hiding archive availability, omitting acquisition adequacy or removing the unchanged clinical status. Those facts make the current key fair; a stronger item needs a different clinical decision.

title: Source-control route for a localized postoperative pelvic abscess
fairness: Persistent fever and focal pain during active antibiotics plus the organized gas-containing pelvic collection support source control. Stable physiology, no generalized peritonitis and the assessed access anatomy favor image-guided drainage over continued antibiotics without drainage or immediate operative exploration.

The two steps are recognizing that persistent illness reflects a drainable localized source despite stable circulation, then choosing an appropriate route from the access geometry and distribution of illness. These are high-yield surgical source-control decisions.

The description of bowel and major vessels relative to the posterior plane is necessary procedural evidence, not a generic 'drainage is available' permission. 'Pelvic' appears in both drainage options, and the task does not name the preferred route. No meaningful wording, absolute or convergence shortcut was identified.

The IV-only CT is not claimed to exclude a bowel leak. No enteric contrast is required merely to make initial percutaneous drainage defensible in this represented stable localized scenario. The explanation appropriately preserves reassessment and possible operation for an uncontrolled source or deterioration; it does not overstate what this scan proves.

The update supplies the relevant CT result and current treatment/physiology, so this node stands alone with the presentation. After the archive-review node it also follows coherently: the newly reviewed images change the next decision. Earlier feedback teaches image adequacy, not the drainage answer.
suggestions: Retain the clinical course, access anatomy and distinction between no generalized peritonitis and proof of no leak. Do not replace those observations with an authored conclusion that the collection is 'suitable for drainage'.

title: Antibiotic endpoint despite mild residual leukocytosis

cues.why: The key is shorter than either continuation plan. This is a limited option-length cue, but a stop order naturally needs fewer words than a conditional continuation endpoint; it does not independently establish the correct answer. Do not add filler to the key merely to equalize length.

fairness: The record gives documented source control without ongoing leakage, four days of active treatment after drainage, substantial clinical recovery and immunocompetence. A slightly elevated but substantially falling leukocyte count does not by itself make continued treatment the best of these options. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified in the proposed stopping decision.

The two steps are interpreting the residual laboratory abnormality in the context of recovery and controlled infection, then applying a treatment endpoint rather than waiting for complete laboratory normalization. The elevated count is a credible resident trap; adequate source control is a necessary premise, not an inference that must be hidden.

Repeat CT before stopping is weaker than the leukocyte-normalization distractor because the patient is asymptomatic with documented source control, but it still represents a recognizable demand for radiographic resolution. All options address when to stop the same antibiotic course.

The explanation appropriately makes source control and recovery part of the endpoint, rather than teaching a universal fixed duration for every abdominal infection. Exact applicability remains for clinician sign-off; this review does not introduce a new duration or threshold.

The later clinic update resets the timeline clearly and supplies drainage, elapsed treatment, source-control status and current findings. It stands alone despite the historical fever in the shared presentation. The earlier drainage feedback says to continue antibiotics at the source-control stage but does not give this later stopping answer.
Antibiotic duration after adequate source control is high yield. This is moderate application of a familiar principle, not a hard item.
suggestions: Optionally tighten all three labels to similarly concise endpoint plans, without concealing the distinction between stopping now, waiting for leukocyte normalization and waiting for repeat imaging.
Keep the mild residual leukocytosis and documented recovery; removing the competing laboratory signal would turn this into uncomplicated short-course recall.
